analysis.one_liner: Removes federal criminal penalties for marijuana and reinvests savings in communities hit hardest by drug arrests.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Cory Booker with eight cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would take marijuana off the federal list of banned drugs, wiping out federal criminal penalties for growing, selling, or carrying it. It would require federal courts to erase past convictions for marijuana use or possession and allow resentencing for people still in prison for marijuana offenses. It would also penalize states that arrest or jail minorities and low-income people for marijuana at higher rates than others, cutting some federal law enforcement money and shifting it into a fund for job training, reentry services, and health programs in communities most affected by drug enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: The main winners are people caught up in federal marijuana enforcement — mostly defendants and incarcerated people, who are disproportionately Black and low-income. People with federal marijuana convictions would get their records cleared, and people still serving sentences could ask for shorter ones. Communities with high arrest rates would get job training, reentry services, expungement help, libraries, youth programs, and health education through a new Community Reinvestment Fund, authorized at $500 million a year through 2042. State-legal marijuana businesses would also gain a clearer legal footing, since growing and selling marijuana would no longer be a federal crime.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with marijuana convictions and affected communities

how_it_helps.text: It removes marijuana from Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act, eliminating federal criminal penalties for importing, exporting, manufacturing, distributing, or possessing with intent to distribute marijuana.
Every federal court must expunge convictions for marijuana use or possession entered before the law's enactment, clearing records that can block jobs and housing.
People still serving federal prison sentences for marijuana offenses can ask for a hearing and potentially be resentenced under the new, penalty-free law.

States with racially or economically disproportionate marijuana arrest or incarceration rates lose eligibility for federal prison construction and staffing funds and face up to a 10% cut to Byrne justice assistance grants, with the withheld money redirected to the Community Reinvestment Fund.

The Community Reinvestment Fund, authorized at $500 million per year for fiscal years 2020 through 2042, would pay for job training, reentry services, expungement expenses, libraries, community centers, youth programs, and health education in communities most affected by drug enforcement.
Individuals aggrieved by a state's disproportionate arrest or incarceration rates could sue in federal court to force the funding penalty.

analysis.who_pays: States that keep marijuana illegal while enforcing it unevenly would bear the cost, losing some federal law enforcement grant money and prison construction funds. Federal and local law enforcement agencies would lose a criminal enforcement mission and its associated funding streams. Taxpayers would fund the Community Reinvestment Fund's authorizations if Congress appropriated the money.
analysis.who_pays_short: Non-legalizing states and law enforcement agencies

drawbacks.text: The bill simply strikes marijuana from the controlled substances schedules and related penalty provisions; it contains no federal framework for regulating sales, potency, labeling, or age limits, leaving products unregulated at the federal level.

States with disproportionate marijuana enforcement would face up to a 10% reduction in Byrne justice assistance grants and loss of prison construction and staffing funds, money that funds local policing operations.
The Community Reinvestment Fund depends on annual appropriations; its $500 million-a-year authorization would deliver nothing unless Congress later votes the money.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core changes — federal decriminalization, record clearing, and resentencing — would directly lift burdens from people with criminal records and their families, and the enforcement-funding penalty gives states a concrete reason to stop unequal enforcement. The honest tradeoffs are that descheduling comes with no federal regulatory structure for a commercial market, and the community reinvestment money is only authorized, not guaranteed. Whether the funding penalty is a fair pressure tactic or an overreach depends on how much weight one gives to local law enforcement needs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the Marijuana Justice Act of 2019 in the Senate on February 28, 2019, joined by seven Democratic cosponsors and one Independent.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day it was introduced; no further action was taken.
The bill never received a committee hearing, markup, floor vote, or House counterpart action, and it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The outcome leaves federal marijuana penalties, past convictions, and existing sentences exactly as they were, so the status quo of federal prohibition continues unchanged. State-legal marijuana businesses still operate in a legal gray zone, and no state faced the funding penalty for unequal enforcement.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal marijuana prohibition stayed in place

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, proposing federal marijuana decriminalization, expungement of past convictions, and community reinvestment grants.

for.name: Sens. Wyden, Merkley, Warren, Harris, Gillibrand, Sanders, and Bennet
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill alongside its Democratic sponsor; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee (Republican-led majority)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred on the day of introduction; the committee took no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters — eight Democrats and one Independent — were from one party; the bill attracted no Republican cosponsors and died in the Republican-led Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote.

industries.note: Removing marijuana from the controlled substances schedules would eliminate federal criminal exposure for a market already legal under state law, letting growers and sellers operate without federal trafficking liability. Consumers in legal states would face no federal risk from a product they can already buy.

industries.industry: Prison construction and jail staffing contractors
industries.note: The bill bars federal prison and jail construction and staffing funds from states with disproportionate marijuana enforcement, shrinking a funding stream these contractors depend on. The same penalty is what pushes states toward fairer enforcement, so the industry's loss is the public's gain.

industries.industry: Federal and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Agencies lose marijuana as a criminal enforcement category and non-legalizing states lose up to 10% of Byrne justice assistance grants, but grant money withheld from penalized states is redirected to community programs rather than eliminated. The enforcement interest here runs against the people the arrests fall on.
